subject: Throughput sizing follow-up: Finex peak vs steady-state
messages:
From: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.com>
To: James Lee <james.lee@finexhealth.com>
Cc: Rafael Mendes <rafael.mendes@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: Sat, 05 Dec 2026 14:02:00 -0800
Subject: Follow-up: throughput / latency targets from today’s call

Hi James — thanks again for the time today. Quick recap and a few clarifying items so we can size capacity and give an initial quote. I attached a lightweight calc (throughput_calc_v1.xlsx) and a 1‑page summary.

Recap of what we heard from Finex:
- Peak burst QPS: ~120 req/s (short bursts up to ~5 minutes)
- Steady-state QPS: 10–18 req/s (diurnal baseline)
- Average request size: ~350 input tokens + ~150 output tokens => ~500 tokens per request (planning number)
- Concurrency: expected ~220 sessions actively streaming at peak; steady-state concurrency ~40
- Streaming: yes — partial results as tokens are generated; client requires first token delivered <150ms and 95th pctl first-byte <300ms
- SLO ask: 95th pctl latency for streaming first token <= 300ms; tail (99th) target is softer (<= 600ms) but would like guidance on tradeoffs

Questions / asks for you so we can finalize sizing:
1) Can you confirm the average tokens/request (500) and whether outputs will typically be <256 tokens or often 512+?
2) Are peak bursts predictable (e.g., payroll cutoffs) or more random?
3) Any existing hard constraints on concurrency per user/session (e.g., single long-lived connection vs many short requests)?

Initial sizing notes (attached calc):
- If we assume 120 QPS * 500 tokens/request = 60k tokens/sec peak.
- With batch-friendly serving and quantized model, a single g5.12x-like GPU can achieve ~8–12k tokens/sec depending on model and sequence length. That suggests ~6–8 GPUs to cover sustained peak with headroom for autoscale and redundancy.
- For low-latency streaming first-byte targets we recommend reserving capacity (dedicated nodes) and avoiding excessive batching for the first token — we can use fast-path inference for first-token latency and batch for subsequent tokens.

Next steps: please confirm the answers above and attach any telemetry (sample traffic shape by minute or histogram) if available. Would you like us to size two options: a cost-optimized baseline (best-effort tails) and a performance SLA baseline (tight 95/99 SLOs)?

Thanks — happy to hop back on with Rafael for the technical sizing deep-dive.

Best,
Neha Kapoor
Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
neha.kapoor@redwood.com
+1 (415) 555-0123

Attachments: throughput_calc_v1.xlsx (spreadsheet, roughs), finex_summary.pdf (one-pager)

From: James Lee <james.lee@finexhealth.com>
To: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.com>
Cc: Priya Shah <priya.shah@finexhealth.com>
Date: Sat, 05 Dec 2026 15:00:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Follow-up: throughput / latency targets from today’s call

Thanks Neha — this is great, and the calc helps. Quick answers:
- Confirm average tokens/request ~= 500. Output tails can spike to ~800 tokens for long-form summaries (~5% of requests).
- Bursts are mostly predictable (end-of-day processing windows and weekly report runs) but we sometimes get random bursts tied to product incidents.
- Concurrency: we maintain long-lived streaming sessions for ~30% of users; others are short-lived requests. So mix of long and short.

Can you include an option that shows cost delta if we target 95th pctl first-byte = 300ms vs more aggressive 99th pctl = 300ms? We have procurement sensitivity to both capacity and run-rate.

We’re good to schedule the technical deep-dive — Dec 9th morning PST would work.

—James
James Lee
Head of Platform Engineering, Finex Health
james.lee@finexhealth.com

From: Rafael Mendes <rafael.mendes@redwood.com>
To: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.com>, James Lee <james.lee@finexhealth.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: Sun, 06 Dec 2026 10:12:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Follow-up: throughput / latency targets from today’s call

Thanks — nice summary. A few concrete sizing proposals and tradeoffs: 

1) Baseline math (using James numbers):
- Peak tokens/sec = 120 QPS * 500 tokens = 60,000 tokens/sec
- If average GPU throughput (quantized LlamaX-13B profile) = ~10k tokens/sec sustained per GPU => ~6 GPUs to handle sustained peak.
- Allow 25–30% headroom for autoscale + redundancy => recommend provisioning 8 GPUs for peak SLA option; 5 GPUs for cost-optimized.

2) Latency / streaming strategy:
- For first-token <150–300ms: use a fast-path inference configuration (no cross-request batching for initial token, pre-warmed kernels, KV-cache pooling) — this costs more per-request because we reduce batching efficiency.
- For steady tokens after the first: we can batch and use continuous generation paths to recover cost. This gives a good compromise between first-byte SLO and per-token cost.

3) Concurrency considerations:
- Long-lived sessions (220 concurrent streams) increase memory/KV cache pressure. Ensure instance types have >=512GB memory if using large context windows, or split sessions across pods to keep per-pod cache within budget.

4) Tail-SLO tradeoffs:
- 95th pctl = 300ms: achievable with reserved capacity + modest overprovisioning (the 8‑GPU recommendation).
- 99th pctl = 300ms: expensive — requires >40% extra headroom and aggressive autoscale warm pools to avoid cold-start spikes. Recommend making 99th pctl a contractual SLA only after pilot.

I’ll update the attached calc with two scenarios (5 GPU cost-optimized, 8 GPU SLA) and include estimated monthly run-rate using your expected utilization. Also adding a row for expected tokens/sec-to-GPU mapping by model variant and quantization level.

If helpful, we can include a quick simulation of burst arrival patterns (Poisson vs scheduled) — that will show probability of autoscale events and cost implications.

Neha / Marissa — I’d suggest we capture the sample minute-by-minute traffic histogram before the deep-dive so we can size warm-pools accurately. James — can you share a 1–2 week traffic histogram?

Thanks,
Rafael Mendes
Senior Solutions Architect | Redwood Inference
rafael.mendes@redwood.com
